title: Triangulation: losing a tempo on purpose
summary: When the position would win with the opponent to move, walk your king around a triangle to hand him the move.

steps.md:
In pawn endings, **zugzwang** often decides: the same position wins with the opponent to move and only draws with you to move. If your king has more room than his, you can **lose a tempo**:

- **Triangulation:** your king makes three moves around a triangle of adjacent squares (e.g. g4-h4-g3-g4) and returns to the same square, while the enemy king, short of space, can only shuttle between two squares. After three moves the original position is back, but **with the opponent to move**.
- A related trick: step to a square that takes away the enemy king's waiting square, so that he has no neutral move.

Always ask first: "Who would be in zugzwang in this position, and can I pass the move?"

steps.prompt: White to move. With Black to move here, ...Ke7 would be a harmless waiting move. Take that waiting move away.
steps.explain: **57.Kf8!** Now e7 touches your king, so the black king has no neutral square: 57...f6 (king moves drop the f7-pawn) 58.Kg7 fxg5 59.fxg5 Kf5 60.Kh6, and Black is in zugzwang again: the g6-pawn falls. You transferred the move to Black by controlling his shuttle square.

steps.prompt: Black to move. White's king on h3 is almost stalemated; White has only pawn moves left. Lose a tempo with your king.
steps.explain: **41...Kg1!** and back **42...Kf2** after 42.g3: the king returns to f2, and White, who had only pawn moves, had to change his structure. After 43.gxf4 gxf4 44.Kg4 Ke3 Black's king invades and wins f3. A two-square shuffle works when the opponent has no waiting moves at all.

steps.md: White to move. White wants his king on g4 with Black to move, so that the black king (shuttling between e4/f5 type squares) must give way. Watch the triangle **g4-h4-g3** in the solution.

steps.prompt: White to move. Win the h-pawn, then triangulate to put Black in zugzwang.
steps.explain: **48.Kf5 h4 49.Kg4 Kf6 50.Kxh4 Kf5 51.Kg3! Ke4 52.Kg4!** The white king went g4-h4-g3-g4 (a triangle) while the black king could only go f5-e4: the same kind of position has arisen, but now **Black is to move**. Every king move gives way: either the f-pawn advances (f4-f5) or the white king enters. Triangulation won the zugzwang.

steps.question: What does triangulation achieve?
choices: It returns to the same position with the opponent to move
It gains the opposition in every position
steps.explain: Three king moves around a triangle versus two shuttling moves: the position repeats, but the side to move has changed. It works only when your king has a triangle of safe squares and the enemy king does not.

steps.question: Why can the defender not simply triangulate back?
choices: His king lacks the room: the squares around it are controlled by pawns or the enemy king, so he can only shuttle between two squares
Triangulation is only allowed for White
steps.explain: Space is the resource. If the defender also has a triangle, the tempo battle continues (corresponding squares, stage 5). Typical error: trying to triangulate when your own king has no safe triangle.

steps.prompt: Play the triangulation position against the engine and promote a pawn.
steps.explain: Take the h-pawn, triangulate with g4-h4-g3-g4 to win the zugzwang, then invade and win the black pawns.

steps.md: **Retrieval check.** Define triangulation in one sentence. In the last example, which three squares formed the triangle? (g4, h4, g3.) Before using it, what must you check? (That the position is a zugzwang for the side to move, and that your king has a safe triangle while the enemy king does not.)
